title: Die Another Day
full_review:
The 20th official James Bond movie, "Die Another Day" (MGM), breaks new ground in that 007's cover is blown and he is tortured and left to rot in a North Korean prison for more than a year -- all before the opening credits roll.

With New Zealand director Lee Tamahori at the helm, the action and intrigue unreel at a furious pace, with death-defying stunts so preposterous one can only laugh and go with the flow. It's unquestionably mindless escapist entertainment, but entertain it does as the story zips from Korea to Hong Kong, London, Havana, Iceland and back to where it started.

And this time Bond (Pierce Brosnan) is not quite agent 007. Released in a prisoner exchange, he is virtually dismissed when he reports back to his London superior, M (Judi Dench, marvelous as ever), as he may have revealed secrets when drugged by his torturers.

Infuriated, Bond sets out on his own to identify who betrayed him and soon teams with an American agent who is as strong, sexy and smart as he is. Jinx (Halle Berry) comes slinking out of the sea (as did early Bond girl Ursula Andress in "Dr. No") in Havana and they are soon entangled in more ways than one.

The villains include Zao (Rick Yune), whose scarred visage is studded with diamonds, courtesy of Bond exploding a diamond-filled attache case in his face, and Graves (Toby Stephens), a faux philanthropist whose new sun-like invention is the world's newest superweapon. Bond learns Graves' assistant Miranda (Rosamund Pike) is actually an British operative before the action moves to Iceland, where Graves is introducing his invention at a stunning palace carved entirely of ice.

Bond and Jinx are soon separately in mortal danger, and while the traitor is unmasked the agents' survival is unlikely as the primo bad guy escapes with the invention, returning to Korea ready to provoke a nuclear response should his megalomaniac demands be shunned.

The movie is simply a series of spectacular set-pieces done in visual terms that amount to luscious eye candy. The characterizations on the other hand are ludicrous; no one seems to be remotely human. The five leads all possess superhuman strength, speed and stamina. The violence is largely stylized, but in such quantity it barely fits in the PG-13 rating, not to mention the obligatory brief bedroom scenes with superstud Bond and his willing women -- all part of the fantasy that continues to draw such a loyal audience.

It is of concern that all the mayhem and explosions are made to look exciting but, since it appears much more fantastic than realistic, it isn't as objectionable as gritty, in-your-face violence.

The cast is up to the job with Brosnan and Berry playing well off one another, but the sprinklings of double entendres are so obvious and lame they are an embarrassment. The icy chases are pretty impressive, if patently absurd, and one gasps when Jinx dives backward into the sea, but at other times the shadows of "Mission Impossible" and "The Matrix" loom large as the Bond franchise tries to stay hip and with-it so many decades after its inception.

With its stunning visuals and sky-high action quotient, James is certain to live on to die another day.

Due to several brief sexual encounters, much stylized violence and mayhem and an instance of profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
